chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) judged regarding a man who was brought by two men who said, 'This one stole an armor.' The man began to adjure him when he looked at the evidence, saying, 'By Allah, if the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) were here, he would never have cut my hand.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'And why not?' He said, 'His Lord would inform him that I am innocent, so he would acquit me based on my innocence.' When he saw his adjuring, he called the two witnesses and said, 'Fear Allah and do not cut the man's hand unjustly,' and he adjured them. Then he said, 'Let one of you cut his hand while the other holds it.' When they approached the place to cut his hand, the people crowded until they mixed together. When they were mixed, they sent the man into the crowd of people until he was mixed with them. The one against whom they had testified came and said, 'O Amir al-Mu'minin, the two men testified against me unjustly. When the people crowded and mixed, they sent me away and fled. If they had been truthful, they would not have sent me away.' Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said, 'Whoever points me to these two, I will punish them severely.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali (peace be upon him) verify the truthfulness of witnesses in a theft case?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates how Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) employed a sophisticated judicial test of *zann* (probability) over *yaqin* (certainty) by inviting the witnesses to cut his own hand, thereby exposing their perjury through their immediate acceptance of the risk. This incident highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the threat of *qisas* (retaliation) for the accuser serves as a powerful mechanism to verify the truthfulness of witnesses in theft cases, moving beyond rigid literalism to practical justice.
